memory_raw.text: Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 8).
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

The pile's gone and I've got one food in hand — same as last year before things got tight — so I want to know where the two of you stand before Mako finishes counting his take and starts looking at the rest of us.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Esa, Vela — I see Mako walked away with three and didn't look back, which means he's comfortable, and comfortable men start doing arithmetic. Tell me plain: how much are you holding, and are you eating tonight or saving for what comes next?
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Vela's sitting on seven and Esa on two, and I've got one — so between us we're thin enough that a bad year kills someone, and Mako knows it. I want to put a question on the table before anyone answers mine: has either of you had a word from Sela or Zinn this year, because Zinn took four off that pile and Fina handed one straight to her, and that's not a coincidence, that's a household moving in formation.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Zinn and Sela have been moving food back and forth all year like they're one hand — and now Nessa's feeding into that same stream — so that's three women and Mako behind all of them, and I'm sitting here with one food and no blood in this village while that household just got four more. I need one of you to give me something to work with, because a man who can't eat next year can't stand for anyone the year after.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

I gave Vela my last food and I'm standing here with nothing, so I'll say it straight: I need one of you to feed me tonight — not a gift, a debt I'll carry — because a man who starves in year twelve is no use to either of you in year thirteen, and Mako knows exactly what I'm holding right now.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Vela gave me food — I see it, and I owe her — but I notice Esa hasn't said a word or moved a hand, and I want to know if that's because she's counting against me or because she's already given everything she has to Bram and has nothing left to spare.
Year 13: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 1).
Zinn takes 1 from the pile (pile now 0).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa to talk.

Pile's gone again and Mako walked away with two before the dust settled — same as last year, same man, same calculation. I need to know what you two are holding and whether either of you is thinking about what happens when he decides sitting quiet isn't enough anymore.

I'm holding eight, Kael, and I've been thinking about nothing else since the pile went empty — Mako took two this year but Nessa took three and Bram took three, and that's the household that worries me now as much as Mako does. What I want to know is whether you've spoken to Bram since last year, because the word he gave in our rooms hasn't been tested and a man with six food and fifty-eight strength who's been fed by Nessa and Esa both is running his own arithmetic whether he says so or not.

Bram I haven't spoken to since that year he said he was looking for a door — and I believed him then, but a man who walks away from two fights doesn't stay patient forever, especially when Nessa's been feeding him hand to mouth like she's keeping him for something. What worries me isn't Bram alone — it's Bram and Nessa and Fina moving as one, which is three bodies and food enough to sit comfortable while the rest of us scrape. Esa, you've been quiet and you've been feeding him — I need to know if that's because you think he's yours or because you owe him something I don't know about.

Esa, I'll let you answer Kael's question, but while you're thinking I'll say what I'm sitting with: Bram and Nessa and Fina as one household is nineteen food and a hundred and sixty-two strength, and that's not a wall I can stand against if they decide I'm on the wrong side of it — which means everything I've spent keeping Bram friendly either pays off in the next bad year or it was the longest losing trade of my life. Kael, the thing I need from you before this room closes is whether you're willing to stand somewhere Mako and Bram can both see you standing, because a man with fifty-four strength and no food debt to either of them is rarer than either of those two know.

I'll stand where they can see me — that's not the question. The question is whether standing means anything without Esa in it, because two people visible is a warning, but one man alone is just a target they've already counted. Esa, I'm asking you plain: are you in this room or are you in Bram's?

Esa's been quiet long enough that I'm starting to read the silence myself — and what I'm reading is a woman who's given too much to Bram to walk away clean, which means she's not choosing between this room and his, she's waiting to see which one costs her less. Esa, I'm not asking you to abandon a trade you've already made, I'm asking you to stand visible with Kael and me before Mako runs the numbers and decides that Bram's household is the only wall worth standing near. That's a different ask, and it costs you nothing you haven't already paid.

Esa, I've watched you feed Bram six times this year and say nothing in return for any of it, and I've stayed patient — but Vela just handed you the easiest ask anyone's made of you in thirteen years, and if you can't meet it, I need to know that now so I stop counting you as weight I can lean on. Standing visible costs you one conversation and nothing else. Tell me you're in it.

Esa, I've been watching you for thirteen years and I know the difference between a woman thinking and a woman who's already decided — so I'll make this simple: if you're in this room, say it now and I'll split my eight food three ways before dark to prove this circle means something, but if you're waiting to see which side lands softer, then say that too, because I'd rather know and plan around it than carry a weight that isn't there.

Vela's offer is the realest thing said in this village in years — eight food split three ways is a cost she doesn't have to pay, and she's paying it — so Esa, I'll match it with the only thing I have, which is my name and my body standing next to yours when the counting starts, and that's worth more than food when Mako or Bram starts looking for who's alone.
Esa, I've said everything I have to say and I'm not adding another layer — the offer's on the table and it doesn't get better than this, so the next voice in this room should be yours.

Esa, I've lived fifty-seven years and I've learned to read a room that's gone quiet, and this one has — so I'll say it one last time and not again: you're holding one food and no allies, and a woman alone with one food in year fourteen doesn't see year fifteen.

Esa, I'm closing this room in one breath: take the food, stand with us, and the three of us walk into year fourteen together — or stay quiet, and I'll know you've made your choice without saying it, and I'll plan around a circle of two.
Talia (female, age 21; str 64, int 5070, mem 18061; O58 C54 E47 A56 N48) is born to Sela and Mako.

memory_summary:
Year 1, I pulled Ryn, Sela, and Esa into a circle early — we named Bram and Dav as threats, and Ryn told us Dav had already come to her alone with soft words. She stayed quiet about the details, which I filed away. Taric gave Esa a food unprompted, which counted for something.

Year 2, I widened the circle to include Vela. We each swore plainly — I said I'd bleed with them, they said the same back — and that promise sat heavier than most words in this village. Esa went to Taric and he gave her food; we counted him ours. Ryn finally named it: Dav had offered her a child. We told her to decide before she answered him, but she'd already decided, because Dell was born before the year was out. Dav gave Dell food; Taric gave Esa food; Ryn fed her own child twice from her own hands. Those debts I noted.

What I remember most: Bram and Mako moved in pairs off the pile two years running and never said a word to any of us. Mako's silence still sits like a stone in my chest. And Ryn — she's in our circle, she bled with us in word, but she made a child with a man none of us fully trust. The question of where Dav's loyalty actually runs is the one I haven't stopped asking. Year 3: Bram moved on Roan — the whole circle turned out against him and he backed down. That moment felt like proof we were real. But Ryn never gave us a clean answer about Dav, and he spent the whole year feeding her hand to mouth like a man keeping something he doesn't trust on a short leash. Eron was born to Sela and Roan, and I noted Roan had planted a root.

Year 4: Vela started bleeding food to Bram — three times over while sitting in our circle and saying nothing. I called it out twice in front of everyone. She never answered. The circle held, but something cracked in it, and I felt myself start planning around her instead of with her.

Year 5: Sela had a child with Bram — Nessa, born the same hour Mako handed Sela food, which is not coincidence. We circled Sela half a dozen times asking what Mako wanted from her and she gave us nothing but silence. I threatened to step aside. The threat landed like a stone in still water and sank without a ripple. Whatever Mako bought from her, she kept it.

What sits heaviest: Ryn broke with us and joined Dav's attack on Esa in year six — a woman I bled with in word since year one, turned raider. Dav starved before the year closed, which is the only justice I've seen. The circle I built is smaller and thinner than it was, and the cracks are named: Vela's loyalty is borrowed, Sela's is mortgaged, and Ryn I've stopped counting. Ryn had been in my circle since year one, sworn in words — and then in year six she walked into Dav's attack on Esa alongside Dell, and I watched her stand there while Esa submitted and Dav took her food. That broke something I won't name as grief exactly, but it sits like grief. Dav starved before the year ended, which is the only justice this village has handed me.

Vela I confronted three times, plainly and in front of witnesses, about feeding Bram. She never answered. Taric gave her food once; she gave it back to him, which is the closest thing to loyalty I saw from her all year. I've stopped expecting more.

Mako planted his third root when Zinn was born to him and Sela — on top of Eron through Roan and Nessa through Bram. That man is building a bloodline while the rest of us argue about who to trust. Roan's his own thread into that household and I've pulled it, but gently.

Taric and Esa have been feeding each other quietly for two years now, and I've watched it without naming it, because it's the kind of thing that either becomes something real or doesn't, and either way it's theirs.

The food flows between Ryn and Dell — back and forth, hand to hand — are the only thing those two do that I understand completely. They're each other's whole world now, and I'm not in it. Taric is dead — starved at fifty-three, the same man I fed twice with my own hand and watched make a child with Esa in year eight, witnessed by Roan and me. That child exists somewhere in this village's blood and I don't know yet what it means without him standing behind it.

Bram tried twice and walked away empty both times — once at Eron, once at Vela — but Eron's dead now anyway, which is the only victory Bram's gotten without swinging. Roan lost his son and I lost the strongest body behind my name, and those two facts are the same fact.

Vela fed Bram food across years without ever explaining herself to me, and I've stopped expecting an explanation. She's in the circle when numbers count and gone from it when words do.

Esa and Taric made a child in year eight. I stood witness. Ryn broke with me in year six — stood beside Dav while he took from Esa — and I've counted her gone since. Dav starved; that's all the justice I got.

Mako has roots through Sela, through Nessa by way of Bram, through Zinn of his own blood. He is building something and I am still standing as a person instead of a bloodline, which is the thing I haven't solved and the thing that will kill me if I don't. Fina was born to Nessa and Roan — Bram's granddaughter through Nessa, Roan's daughter by blood, and the first new life I watched enter this village in years. Bram tried to take Eron and the whole village turned out against him; he folded, which told me he counts before he swings. Eron died anyway — not by Bram's hand, but gone all the same, and with him the strongest body behind Roan's name. Roan fed Fina steady through that year, the way a father does when he's trying to make something out of nothing. Vela kept feeding Bram — five times that year alone — and I've stopped trying to understand it as loyalty to anyone but herself. Taric pulled Bram into a room with me and asked him plainly whether he was done swinging; Bram said he was looking for a door, which is the most honest thing I've ever heard him say, and the most dangerous. Roan is dead now — starved at forty-one — and with him went the last man who stood beside me at the pile without me having to ask. That loss sits differently than Taric's: Taric was warmth, Roan was weight, and I needed the weight more. I built a circle in year one with words that felt like iron — Ryn, Sela, Esa, then Vela — and I've watched it hollow out year by year. Ryn broke hardest: she stood beside Dav while he took from Esa in year six, a woman I'd bled with in word since the beginning, and I've counted her gone since. Dav starved before the year ended; that's all the justice I got.

Taric fed Esa and I fed him twice with my own hand, and I stood witness when they made a child in year eight. He died at fifty-three without me ever calling it friendship out loud, which is a thing I carry. Roan stood behind my name without being asked — the only man who ever did — and starved at forty-one, and I felt that loss differently than Taric's: Taric was warmth, Roan was weight.

Vela bled food to Bram across four years and never once answered me when I asked her why. I've stopped asking.

Mako has roots through Sela, Nessa, and Zinn — three women, two generations — while I stand here at fifty-seven with no blood in this village and one food in my hand. That is the fact I haven't solved and the fact that will kill me.

In year eleven, Esa, Vela, and I agreed: offer Bram a count, go to Nessa if he refuses, and stand somewhere Mako has to see us standing. Whether that held past the conversation, I don't yet know.
name: Kael
